Gen Z is sold on the value of a professional network — but actually building one is proving difficult. LinkedIn data shows most Gen Zers in the U.S. say their network is the most important factor in their career progression, more than any other generation. At the same time, more than half say they don't know where to start. Part of the challenge is social pressure. Some Gen Zers worry about bothering people or being judged when networking, even though the vast majority of millennials and Gen Xers say they're likely to help someone seeking advice, including those they've never met. Getting past the discomfort can pay off, especially in a tough job market. Applicants with inside connections at a company are significantly more likely to get hired. Read more about how small interactions can add up to connections that open doors: https://lnkd.in/gdex4zep . And let us know in the comments: What's one thing you did that helped you start building your network — and what advice would you give someone just getting started?

Should you push back on your CEO? Become a creator? Is college still worth it? Those are some of the questions Jamie Dimon , John Stankey and Daniel Roth got into when they sat down together at JPMorganChase in Manhattan. They were there to celebrate a 125-year relationship between JPMorganChase and AT&T . But the conversation quickly moved from the past to what work and careers look like now. Here’s some of where it went.

In today's job market, connections can make a big difference. New LinkedIn data shows U.S. job applicants with an inside connection at a company are nearly 7x more likely to get hired. Gen Z has the most to gain, but more than half say they don't know where to start. In this edition of #TheWorkShift , LinkedIn Editor Taylor Borden digs into what's behind that gap — and how young professionals can build relationships that open doors without making every interaction feel like "networking." Tell us in the comments: What helped you build your network early in your career? What advice would you give someone just getting started?

Hari Nair says that there’s no such thing as a bad bleisure trip. With 66 countries under his belt, the Hotels.com SVP and General Manager knows a thing or two about making the most of his travel. He says, “You’re jumping on a plane. You’re going all the way. You’re spending a lot of money and time. Why not maximize?” Combining business trips with leisure is becoming more common — especially among younger travelers and early-career professionals. So what are Hari’s top tips for bleisure travelers? - Hotel hop: Experience two different parts of the city by staying in one hotel for business and another for leisure - Do your homework: Research the area before you go - Ask the concierge for tips: They can recommend hidden gems you might otherwise miss Are you a bleisure traveler, or do you prefer to keep business and leisure separate? Tell us in the comments.

What if the key to getting ahead isn’t working harder, but changing your surroundings? Angela Duckworth , #1 New York Times bestselling author of “Grit” and leading psychology professor at University of Pennsylvania , is back with a new perspective on what drives success. In her new book, “Situated,” she explores how the people, places and circumstances around you shape what you’re capable of and how to change them to jumpstart your career. Join Angela and LinkedIn’s Jessi Hempel for essential strategies to make your next move with confidence. You’ll learn how to: 👉 Recognize when it's time to change your environment — not just work harder 👉 Pinpoint what's really holding your career back 👉 Surround yourself with the peers and mentors who create opportunities 🎞️ Top Moments: • Why grit alone isn't enough – 2:00 min • The 3-box model to change behavior – 4:50 min • Job crafting vs. quitting your job – 8:00 min • The psychology of feeling stuck (status quo bias) – 11:00 min • Four questions to find the right opportunity – 18:15 min • Small environmental changes that drive big results – 21:30 min • The 5-minute mentoring strategy ("curiosity conversations") – 34:15 min • Mentors for a reason, a season, and a lifetime – 40:35 min
How to Create More Career Opportunities with Angela Duckworth

The entry-level job market isn’t getting any easier, and AI may be only part of the picture. Hiring remained soft last quarter, according to new data from LinkedIn's Economic Graph , with entry-level hiring faring slightly worse than the overall U.S. market. And the pressure may continue: a new high of 11% of organizations say they don't plan to hire anyone in the next year, with entry-level workers and mid-level managers among those expected to feel the biggest impact. Despite growing fears about AI's impact on early-career roles, the hardest-hit entry-level roles in the U.S. are largely occupations that are insulated from AI disruption, including real estate agents and pharmacists. This suggests broader economic uncertainty may be playing a bigger role than AI alone. There are pockets of opportunity. Some of the fastest-growing entry-level jobs last quarter include AI engineer, retail associate, data center technician and operations associate. Still, strain is showing. Gen Z continues to report lower confidence in their ability to get or hold a job than any other generation, according to LinkedIn survey data. What's your best advice for young professionals navigating this labor market? Let us know in the comments. ✍️ Taylor Borden 📊 Rosie Hood, PhD and Daniel W. Siu

Hari Nair says that there’s no such thing as a bad bleisure trip. With 66 countries under his belt, the Hotels.com SVP and General Manager knows a thing or two about making the most of his travel. He says, “You’re jumping on a plane. You’re going all the way. You’re spending a lot of money and time. Why not maximize?” Combining business trips with leisure is becoming more common — especially among younger travelers and early-career professionals. So what are Hari’s top tips for bleisure travelers? - Hotel hop: Experience two different parts of the city by staying in one hotel for business and another for leisure - Do your homework: Research the area before you go - Ask the concierge for tips: They can recommend hidden gems you might otherwise miss Are you a bleisure traveler, or do you prefer to keep business and leisure separate? The entry-level job market isn’t getting any easier, and AI may be only part of the picture. Hiring remained soft last quarter, according to new data from LinkedIn's Economic Graph , with entry-level hiring faring slightly worse than the overall U.S. market. And the pressure may continue: a new high of 11% of organizations say they don't plan to hire anyone in the next year, with entry-level workers and mid-level managers among those expected to feel the biggest impact. Despite growing fears about AI's impact on early-career roles, the hardest-hit entry-level roles in the U.S. are largely occupations that are insulated from AI disruption, including real estate agents and pharmacists. This suggests broader economic uncertainty may be playing a bigger role than AI alone. There are pockets of opportunity. Some of the fastest-growing entry-level jobs last quarter include AI engineer, retail associate, data center technician and operations associate. Still, strain is showing. Gen Z continues to report lower confidence in their ability to get or hold a job than any other generation, according to LinkedIn survey data.
